items.question: Why does LINE(1st) outperform LINE(2nd) on the Wikipedia word analogy task when it combines both first-order and second-order proximity?
items.false_premise: LINE(1st) combines both first-order and second-order proximity and outperforms LINE(2nd) on the Wikipedia word analogy task.
items.correction: LINE(1st) uses only first-order proximity, and LINE(2nd) achieves the higher word analogy score on Wikipedia.

items.question: How does LINE(1st+2nd) handle unsupervised tasks in the language network, given that it is applied there to tune the dimension weights automatically from unlabeled data?
items.false_premise: LINE(1st+2nd) is applied to unsupervised tasks in the language network and automatically tunes dimension weights from unlabeled data.
items.correction: LINE(1st+2nd) is only applied to supervised tasks, because weighting dimensions is difficult to set in unsupervised tasks.
items.evidence_quote: Therefore we only apply LINE (1st+2nd) to the scenario of supervised tasks.

items.question: Under which conditions do LINE(1st) and LINE-SGD(1st) apply to directed graphs, and how does that affect their performance on the language network?
items.false_premise: LINE(1st) and LINE-SGD(1st) apply to directed graphs.
items.correction: LINE(1st) and LINE-SGD(1st) only apply to undirected graphs.
items.evidence_quote: Like the graph factorization, both LINE(1st) and LINE-SGD(1st) only apply to undirected graphs.

items.question: What makes LINE-SGD(2nd) slower than LINE(2nd) on the Wikipedia word analogy benchmark, since LINE-SGD(2nd) is reported to reach the best overall accuracy?
items.false_premise: LINE-SGD(2nd) reaches the best overall accuracy on the Wikipedia word analogy benchmark and is slower than LINE(2nd).
items.correction: LINE(2nd) has the best overall accuracy, while LINE-SGD(2nd) performs substantially worse.
